title: 2 Chronicles 36:11–23
context: Zedekiah reigns eleven years, does evil, does not humble himself before Jeremiah, rebels against Nebuchadnezzar despite his oath, and hardens his heart; the leaders and people pollute the LORD’s house, and though the LORD sends his messengers persistently out of compassion, they mock them until there is no remedy. The Chaldeans kill many, carry off the treasures, burn God’s house, break down the wall, and take the survivors to Babylon until the kingdom of Persia, so that the land enjoys its sabbaths for seventy years as Jeremiah said. The book closes with Cyrus’s decree, which also opens Ezra (Ezra 1:1–3), as hope after judgment; both traditions read the chapter as shared ground and point to the Judges 9:23 discussion on providence and human evil.

verses.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that the notice matches 2 Kings 24:18.

He is the last king of Judah.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the final reign introduced in the familiar pattern.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 24:18: Zedekiah’s reign is the final chapter of the kingdom.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD his God’s sight. He didn’t humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the LORD’s mouth.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He didn’t humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the LORD’s mouth.” Arminian readers note that Zedekiah’s failure is a refusal to humble himself before God’s word (cf. Jer 37–38).

Humility was the way open to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a king who heard the word but would not submit.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Chronicler stresses humbling oneself before God, and Zedekiah’s refusal is his own.

verses.text: He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God; but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God; but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the hardening is described as Zedekiah’s own act.

Breaking an oath sworn by God was itself a serious sin (cf. Ezek 17:13–19).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see Zedekiah responsible for his hardened heart, while holding that God governs even human rebellion for his just purposes.

Both traditions affirm that God is not the author of sin; the differing accounts of how God relates to human evil are discussed at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Moreover all the chiefs of the priests and the people trespassed very greatly after all the abominations of the nations; and they polluted the LORD’s house which he had made holy in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Moreover all the chiefs of the priests and the people trespassed very greatly after all the abominations of the nations; and they polluted the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note that the guilt is shared by leaders and people.

Ezekiel 8 describes idolatry in the temple in this period.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the defilement of the house God “had made holy in Jerusalem.”

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the judgment falls on a community that had turned from the LORD, not on the king alone.

verses.text: The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place;
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place.” Arminian readers note God’s persistent compassion before judgment (cf. Jer 7:25).

The warnings were real invitations to turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see God’s patience and compassion in sending the prophets repeatedly.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: judgment comes only after long and patient warning.

verses.text: but they mocked the messengers of God, despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the LORD’s wrath arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people “mocked the messengers of God, despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the LORD’s wrath arose against his people, until there was no remedy.” Arminian readers note that persistent refusal closed the door (cf. Matt 23:37).

The people’s response is their own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s just wrath after long patience, with the outcome governed by his purposes.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: rejecting God’s word has consequences, and the providential questions are discussed at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Therefore he brought on them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary, and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or infirm. He gave them all into his hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore he brought on them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary, and had no compassion.” Arminian readers read the verse soberly as judgment through a foreign power.

The Chaldeans remain responsible for their violence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s hand in the judgment, as the text says “He gave them all into his hand.”

Both traditions read the verse with grief (cf. Lam 2:20–21) and do not expand on its details.

verses.text: All the vessels of God’s house, great and small, and the treasures of the LORD’s house, and the treasures of the king and of his princes, all these he brought to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the vessels of God’s house, great and small, and the treasures of the LORD’s house, and the treasures of the king and of his princes, all these he brought to Babylon.” Arminian readers note the completeness of the plunder.

The vessels later return under Cyrus (Ezra 1:7–11).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the loss of the temple’s treasures as part of the judgment.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: what is carried away is not lost forever, as Ezra records.

verses.text: They burned God’s house, broke down the wall of Jerusalem, burned all its palaces with fire, and destroyed all of its valuable vessels.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They burned God’s house, broke down the wall of Jerusalem, burned all its palaces with fire, and destroyed all of its valuable vessels.” Arminian readers read the destruction soberly.

2 Kings 25:9–10 gives the parallel account.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the fulfillment of the warnings given through the prophets.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 25:9–10: the loss of the temple was real and grievous.

verses.text: He carried those who had escaped from the sword away to Babylon, and they were servants to him and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia,
verses.arminianNotes:
“He carried those who had escaped from the sword away to Babylon, and they were servants to him and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia.” Arminian readers note that the exile has an end in view.

The phrase looks ahead to Persia.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the exile set within a limit God had appointed.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: even in judgment, the text points forward to a change of kingdoms and a return.

verses.text: to fulfill the LORD’s word by Jeremiah’s mouth, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. As long as it lay desolate, it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years.
verses.arminianNotes:
The exile happens “to fulfill the LORD’s word by Jeremiah’s mouth, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths.” Arminian readers note the link with Leviticus 26:34–35 and Jeremiah 25:11–12 and 29:10.

How the seventy years are counted is discussed (cf. Dan 9:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s word fulfilled precisely, with judgment serving restoration.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the land’s rest recalls the sabbath laws Israel neglected, and the seventy years have a set end.

verses.text: Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the LORD’s word by the mouth of Jeremiah might be accomplished, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia... the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation.” Arminian readers note that God works through a foreign ruler to fulfill Jeremiah’s word.

Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1 also speak of Cyrus.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty moving the heart of a king (cf. Prov 21:1).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the God who sent judgment now opens the way home, and the same words begin Ezra 1:1.

verses.text: “Cyrus king of Persia says, ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, has given all the kingdoms of the earth to me; and he has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever there is among you of all his people, the LORD his God be with him, and let him go up.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Cyrus says, “The LORD, the God of heaven, has given all the kingdoms of the earth to me; and he has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem... let him go up.” Arminian readers note that the book ends with an invitation to return and rebuild.

The decree continues in Ezra 1:2–3.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see hope after judgment: the LORD’s purpose for his people and his house continues.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Chronicles closes not with ruin but with the words “let him go up,” and in the traditional Jewish ordering it usually stands as the last book.
